nodes.text:
Viral Bronchiolitis

Definition:
Viral bronchiolitis is a common lower respiratory tract infection in infants and young children, characterized by inflammation, edema, and obstruction of the small airways (bronchioles). It is most commonly caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV).

Etiology:

•Most common cause: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV).
•Other pathogens: Rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, adenovirus, and human metapneumovirus.

Epidemiology:

•Affects children under 2 years, with the highest incidence in infants 2-6 months old.
•Seasonal prevalence: Late fall to early spring.

Clinical Features:

1.Early Symptoms (Upper Respiratory):
•Nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, and low-grade fever.
2.Progression (Lower Respiratory):
•Cough, tachypnea, wheezing, crackles, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, and respiratory distress.
•Severe cases may present with hypoxia, cyanosis, or apnea.

Diagnosis:

•Primarily clinical based on history and physical examination.
•Additional testing (for severe or atypical cases):
•Viral PCR or antigen testing from nasopharyngeal swab for RSV or other viruses.
•Chest X-ray: May show hyperinflation, peribronchial thickening, or atelectasis (used in complicated cases).
•Pulse oximetry to monitor oxygen saturation.

Management:

1.Supportive Care (Mainstay):
•Ensure adequate hydration and nutrition.
•Oxygen supplementation for SpO₂ < 90%.
•Nasal suctioning to relieve airway obstruction.
2.Hospitalization Indications:
•Severe respiratory distress.
•Hypoxemia (SpO₂ < 90%).
•Dehydration or inability to feed.
•History of apnea or underlying comorbidities (e.g., prematurity, chronic lung disease).
3.Medications:
•Not routinely recommended: Bronchodilators, corticosteroids, or antibiotics (unless secondary bacterial infection is suspected).
•Trial of bronchodilators may be considered in individual cases.

Complications:

•Apnea (especially in young infants).
•Respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation.
•Secondary bacterial infections, such as pneumonia.
•Long-term: Increased risk of recurrent wheezing or asthma.

Prevention:

•Hygiene Measures: Regular handwashing, avoiding exposure to sick individuals, and cleaning frequently touched surfaces.
•Palivizumab Prophylaxis:
•Recommended for high-risk infants (e.g., premature infants, chronic lung disease, or congenital heart disease).
•Annual influenza vaccination for all eligible children and caregivers.

Prognosis:

•Most children recover fully within 1-2 weeks, though symptoms such as cough may persist for longer. Severe cases may require intensive care but have a good prognosis with appropriate management.
